lessons.title: Photosynthesis and the leaf
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Biology — Photosynthesis, diet and digestion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Write the word and balanced symbol equations for photosynthesis.
Describe the structure of a leaf and how it is adapted for photosynthesis.
Explain the effect of light, carbon dioxide and temperature on the rate and describe the starch test.
reviewNotes: Light intensity ∝ 1/d² is the inverse-square law (assumed for a point source); the bubble numbers are illustrative. Photosynthesis rate curves are schematic.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Photosynthesis
blocks.md: **Photosynthesis** is the process by which green plants make **glucose** from **carbon dioxide** and **water** using **light energy** absorbed by **chlorophyll** in chloroplasts: **carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen**, or 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. Light energy is changed into chemical energy stored in glucose. The glucose is used for respiration, stored as **starch**, made into **cellulose** for cell walls, and with nitrates makes **amino acids and proteins**.

blocks.caption: Cross-section of a leaf.
blocks.alt: A leaf section showing the cuticle and upper epidermis, palisade cells with many chloroplasts, spongy mesophyll with air spaces, a vein and the lower epidermis with a stoma.

blocks.title: Leaf adaptations and minerals
blocks.md: The leaf is **thin and flat** (large area, short diffusion path), has **palisade cells** packed with chloroplasts near the light, **air spaces** in the spongy layer for gases, **stomata** with **guard cells** for gas exchange, and **veins**: **xylem** brings water and minerals, **phloem** carries sugars away. Plants also need **nitrate** (for proteins) and **magnesium** (to make chlorophyll) from the soil; shortage of nitrate stunts growth and of magnesium makes leaves yellow.

blocks.caption: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity (schematic).
blocks.alt: A curve that rises steeply and then levels off, with the plateau labelled.

blocks.title: Limiting factors and the starch test
blocks.md: The rate is limited by the factor in **shortest supply**: **light intensity**, **carbon dioxide concentration** or **temperature** (enzymes work best at about 25–35 °C). Once light is no longer limiting, the curve **levels off** (CO₂ or temperature limits). **Starch test**: dip the leaf in boiling water, boil it in ethanol in a hot water bath to remove chlorophyll, rinse, add iodine: **blue-black** means starch.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Plants do respire all the time; they carry out photosynthesis only in the light. Both use gases.
- Never heat ethanol over a flame: use a hot water bath.
- Oxygen is a **product**, not a raw material.

blocks.title: Pondweed bubbles
blocks.statement: A lamp is 10 cm from a pondweed and it gives off 40 bubbles per minute. Light intensity is proportional to 1 ÷ (distance)². Predict the rate at 20 cm if the rate is proportional to the light intensity.
steps: Doubling the distance makes the intensity (1/2)² = 1/4.

blocks.title: Interpret the starch test
blocks.statement: A variegated leaf with green and white parts is tested with iodine after a sunny day. Only the green parts turn blue-black. What does this show?
steps: Green parts contain chlorophyll and make starch.
White parts have no chlorophyll: chlorophyll is needed for photosynthesis.

lessons.title: Food, diet and deficiency diseases
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Biology — Photosynthesis, diet and digestion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: List the food classes, their sources and their functions.
Describe the laboratory tests for starch, reducing sugars, protein and fat.
Explain a balanced diet and name deficiency diseases and their causes.
reviewNotes: Energy values 17 and 37 kJ/g are the usual rounded figures. Deficiency diseases and their causes are standard; health content to be reviewed by a health worker. Content overlaps with form4-biology (food classes) in simplified form.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Food classes
blocks.md:
- **Carbohydrates** (cassava, yam, rice, plantain): energy.
- **Proteins** (beans, fish, eggs, meat, groundnuts): growth and repair.
- **Fats and oils** (palm oil, groundnuts): energy store, insulation, protect organs.
- **Vitamins** (fruit, vegetables) and **minerals** (iron in meat and leaves, calcium in milk and fish): health.
- **Fibre**: moves food through the gut.
- **Water**: solvent, transport, cools the body.

blocks.caption: Energy released per gram of food class (kJ/g).
blocks.alt: A bar chart: carbohydrate 17, protein 17 and fat 37 kilojoules per gram.

blocks.title: Food tests
blocks.md:
- **Starch**: add iodine solution; **blue-black**.
- **Reducing sugar**: heat with **Benedict's solution**; blue → green → yellow → **brick-red**.
- **Protein**: **biuret** test: sodium hydroxide then a little copper sulphate; **purple/violet**.
- **Fat**: rub on paper (translucent stain) or shake with ethanol and add water: **milky white emulsion**.

blocks.title: Balanced diet and deficiency
blocks.md: A **balanced diet** has all the food classes in the right amounts for age, sex and activity. **Kwashiorkor** (protein shortage: swollen belly), **marasmus** (shortage of energy and protein), **scurvy** (vitamin C), **rickets** (vitamin D or calcium: soft bones), **anaemia** (iron) and **goitre** (iodine) are deficiency conditions. Too much energy food leads to **obesity**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Benedict's solution is heated, iodine is not.
- The biuret test is for protein, not for sugar.
- Fibre and water give no energy but are essential.

blocks.title: Energy in a meal
blocks.statement: A meal has 60 g carbohydrate, 20 g protein and 25 g fat. Use 17 kJ/g for carbohydrate and protein and 37 kJ/g for fat. Find the total energy.
steps: Carbohydrate 60 × 17 = 1020 kJ; protein 20 × 17 = 340 kJ; fat 25 × 37 = 925 kJ.

blocks.title: Which test?
blocks.statement: A food sample turns brick-red after heating with Benedict's solution. What does it contain?
steps: Benedict's solution tests for reducing sugars.
Brick-red is the strong positive result.

lessons.title: Digestion and enzymes
lessons.programRef: Form 3 Biology — Photosynthesis, diet and digestion (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the parts of the alimentary canal and their functions.
Name the main digestive enzymes, substrates and products.
Explain the effects of temperature and pH on enzymes and the role of bile and the villi.
reviewNotes: Enzyme activity curve is schematic. 'Bile emulsifies fat' and enzyme locations are standard textbook statements; check whether the syllabus names maltase.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Digestion
blocks.md: **Digestion** is the breakdown of large insoluble food molecules into small soluble ones that can be absorbed. **Physical digestion**: chewing and churning. **Chemical digestion**: **enzymes**, which are **biological catalysts made of protein**. Path: **mouth** (teeth, saliva) → **oesophagus** (peristalsis) → **stomach** (acid, churning) → **small intestine** (digestion and absorption) → **large intestine** (water absorbed) → **rectum** → **anus** (egestion).

blocks.title: Enzymes and what they do
blocks.md: **Amylase** (saliva, pancreas): starch → sugars (maltose, then glucose). **Protease** (stomach, pancreas, small intestine): proteins → **amino acids**. **Lipase** (pancreas, small intestine): fats → **fatty acids and glycerol**. **Bile**, made in the **liver** and stored in the **gall bladder**, is not an enzyme: it **emulsifies fat** into tiny droplets and neutralises stomach acid. The stomach acid (hydrochloric acid) kills germs and gives the right pH for protease.

blocks.caption: Enzyme activity against temperature (schematic).
blocks.alt: A curve that rises to a peak at 37 degrees Celsius, the optimum, then falls to zero as the enzyme is destroyed at high temperature.

blocks.title: Absorption, enzymes and conditions
blocks.md: The small intestine is **long**, with a wall folded into **villi** that have a large surface area, thin walls and a network of **capillaries**, so digested food passes quickly into the blood. Enzymes work best at their **optimum temperature** (about 37 °C in humans) and **pH**; high temperatures **denature** them (their shape is destroyed permanently); low temperatures slow them but do not destroy them. Stomach protease prefers acid; amylase in saliva prefers a nearly neutral pH.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Bile is **not** an enzyme and does not digest fat chemically; it breaks fat into droplets.
- Enzymes are **denatured**, not 'killed', by heat: they are not alive.
- Absorption is not digestion: digestion breaks food down, absorption moves it into the blood.

blocks.title: Which enzyme?
blocks.statement: Name the enzyme and the product when egg white (protein) is digested in the stomach.
steps: The enzyme that digests protein is protease (pepsin).
The final products are amino acids.

blocks.title: Explain the graph
blocks.statement: Using the graph, explain why enzyme activity falls above 40 °C.
steps: High temperature changes the shape of the enzyme (denatures it).
The substrate no longer fits the active site, so the reaction stops.
